label-abacavir: This reading is the F D A prescribing information for Ziagen, which is abacavir, revised November twenty twenty. It matters for Exam four because it is one of the three labels on Dr. Smith's Pharmacogenomics Questions worksheet, discussed on October twenty seventh. Abacavir is a nucleoside analogue H I V one reverse transcriptase inhibitor. It is used with other antiretroviral agents to treat H I V one infection. Dr. Smith said the label has pharmacogenomic information in the boxed warning, dosage and administration, contraindications, and warnings and precautions sections. Item one asks for the gene and variant. The gene is H L A B, and the variant is H L A B fifty seven oh one. Item two: carriers are at higher risk of a serious and sometimes fatal hypersensitivity reaction. The label calls it a multi organ clinical syndrome, and it has included multi organ failure and anaphylaxis. Reactions also occur in patients who do not carry the variant. In class, the answer given was "Multi-organ failure." Item three: the patient is tested, not a tumor. Dr. Smith said, "we're not dealing with tumors with these drugs for carbamazepine and abacavir." The recording ends before items four to eight were worked aloud, so those answers come from the label. Item four: the test is done to prevent a toxicity, not because the drug works less well in carriers. Item five: it is genotyping. The Medication Guide calls it a blood test for the gene variation. Item six: the label names no test or method. It says only to screen for the allele before starting therapy. Item seven: all patients are screened before starting or restarting abacavir, unless a previous assessment is documented. Item eight: a patient who carries H L A B fifty seven oh one must not receive abacavir, because the label lists it as a contraindication. Whatever the test result, the drug is stopped at once if a hypersensitivity reaction is suspected, and never restarted after a reaction. Her main point was the comparison with carbamazepine. She said, "The H L A B gene is involved in both, but it's a different genetic variant for carbamazepine compared to abacavir, same gene." Carbamazepine goes with H L A B fifteen oh two. She said the carbamazepine reaction is in the skin, and the abacavir reaction is "a whole organ hypersensitivity reaction." She said the abacavir problem was first identified as massive skin problems similar to carbamazepine. A negative test for one H L A B variant does not clear the other drug.
label-carbamazepine: This reading is the F D A prescribing information for Tegretol, which is carbamazepine. It matters for Exam four because it is one of the three labels on Dr. Smith's Pharmacogenomics Questions worksheet, discussed on October twenty seventh. Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant and a specific analgesic for trigeminal neuralgia. Dr. Smith said it is "one of our older anti-epileptic medications that we still use." The copy provided is dated July twenty twenty six. In class the date was read out as twenty seventeen. Item one asks for the gene and variant. The first gene is H L A B, with the variant H L A B fifteen oh two. The second is H L A A, with the variant H L A A thirty one oh one. Item two asks what the variants do. Dr. Smith said, "Both of those greatly increase the risk of a patient having this hypersensitivity reaction manifested by skin reactions." She said, "These can be fatal." She said it "makes your skin burn and fall off." The label grades the two differently. It calls H L A B fifteen oh two a strong association with Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, S J S and T E N. It calls H L A A thirty one oh one a moderate association with hypersensitivity reactions. Those include S J S and T E N, maculopapular eruptions, and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms. Item three: the patient is tested, not a tumor, because the variants are inherited. The recording ends before items four to eight were worked aloud, so those answers are from the label. Item four: the test prevents a toxicity. The variants do not change how well the drug controls seizures. Item five: it is genotyping. Item six: for H L A B fifteen oh two the label names a test, high resolution H L A B fifteen oh two typing. It names no test for H L A A thirty one oh one. Item seven: patients with ancestry in genetically at risk populations are screened before starting. H L A B fifteen oh two is found almost exclusively in patients with ancestry across broad areas of Asia. Item eight: a patient positive for H L A B fifteen oh two should not be treated unless the benefits clearly outweigh the risks. For H L A A thirty one oh one, the risks and benefits are weighed. Genotyping must never substitute for clinical vigilance. The drug is stopped at the first sign of a rash unless the rash is clearly not drug related. Abacavir also carries an H L A B warning, but for H L A B fifty seven oh one. She said, "carbamazepine is located in the skin, and for abacavir, it's a whole organ hypersensitivity reaction."
label-trastuzumab: This reading is the F D A prescribing information for Herceptin, which is trastuzumab, revised May twenty twenty six. It matters for Exam four because it is one of the three labels on Dr. Smith's Pharmacogenomics Questions worksheet, discussed on October twenty seventh. It is her example where the tumor is tested, not the patient, and where the test is about efficacy, not toxicity. The label calls Herceptin a Her two neu receptor antagonist. It is indicated in adults for Her two overexpressing breast cancer, and for Her two overexpressing metastatic gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. Item one asks for the gene and variant. The label names the Her two proto-oncogene, which encodes a receptor protein of one hundred eighty five kilodaltons. It names no variant. Dr. Smith said she thinks the one hundred eighty five is the size of the protein. Item two: Herceptin inhibits the proliferation of tumor cells that overexpress Her two, so a Her two negative tumor lacks the drug's target. Item three: the tumor is tested. Dr. Smith said, "So they actually don't genotype people, they're phenotyping the tumor." She said normal cells do not express Her two. Item four: the test is for efficacy. Dr. Smith said, "We want to be sure these patients have the drug's target, which is Her two, before we give them an expensive drug that can cause side effects." Item five: Dr. Smith said, "Usually we do immunohistochemistry to look for the presence of those receptors on those tumor cells." The clinical studies also used F I S H, fluorescence in situ hybridization, for Her two gene amplification. Item six asks whether the F D A names a test. Dr. Smith said the label "a few years ago used to name a certain brand of a kit." She said it no longer does, and that the test needs to be specific and sensitive. The current label names no brand. It asks for F D A authorized tests specific for breast or gastric cancers, done by laboratories with demonstrated proficiency. Item seven: the answer is a tumor type, not an ethnic group. Dr. Smith named breast, metastatic gastrointestinal, and esophageal tumors. The label is narrower: breast cancer, and metastatic gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. Item eight: Dr. Smith said, "If they are Her two positive, they're likely candidates for using trastuzumab. If they're Her two negative, you're not going to use trastuzumab in that patient." The result decides whether the drug is used, not its dose.
cpic-warfarin-2017: This reading is the twenty seventeen C pick guideline for pharmacogenetics guided warfarin dosing. It matters for Exam four because Dr. Smith listed its two figures, and she walked through it in class on October twenty seventh. She said the warfarin guideline had been updated, but the newest version did not open, so the class read the twenty seventeen update. Dr. Smith said these guidelines show "how available genetic test results should be used to optimize drug therapy and not whether tests should be ordered." Figure one shows warfarin's target and how warfarin and vitamin K are metabolized. Both forms of warfarin, R and S, inhibit V K O R C one, the vitamin K epoxide reductase. That limits reduced vitamin K, so G G C X makes fewer active clotting factors. S warfarin is three to five times more potent than R warfarin, and it is metabolized mainly by sip two C nine. Sip four F two removes vitamin K from the vitamin K cycle. In Figure two, without a sip two C nine and V K O R C one genotype, the patient is dosed clinically, without genetic information. Dr. Smith said, "Dose your patient empirically." With a genotype, the patient's self identified ancestry decides the branch. For non African ancestry, the dose is calculated with a published algorithm. The algorithm uses V K O R C one minus 1639 G to A, and sip two C nine star two and star three. That recommendation is graded strong. Sip two C nine star five, star six, star eight, or star eleven lowers the calculated dose by fifteen to thirty percent per allele, an optional recommendation. Sip four F two star three raises it by five to ten percent, also optional. For African ancestry, star five, star six, star eight, and star eleven must be tested first, or the patient is dosed clinically. These variants have their highest frequency in African ancestry. There, an A G or A A result at r s one two seven seven seven eight two three lowers the dose by ten to twenty five percent, graded moderate. No sip four F two recommendation is made for African ancestry. Strong means desirable effects clearly outweigh undesirable ones. Moderate means a close or uncertain balance. Optional means a close balance that allows differences in opinion. Dr. Smith said on October twenty eighth, "you should know which genetic variants we're concerned about and in which populations." Her case questions ask whether all the genotyping was done, and whether the patient needs more or less than the average starting dose. She said a sip two C nine variant and sip four F two star three have "opposite effects on the dose."
naranjo: This reading is the Naranjo Algorithm, a one page questionnaire of ten questions. It matters for Exam four because Dr. Smith's study list says, "Be able to use the Naranjo algorithm." She showed it on October twenty eighth, in the lecture on adverse drug events. It scores how likely it is that one drug caused a patient's adverse reaction. Dr. Smith said, "we have to try to prove the causality to know what drug might be causing the problem." She said the answers come from sitting with the patient and asking when the drugs and the symptoms started, and what other medications they take. Each question is answered yes, no, or do not know, and each answer has set points. Do not know scores zero on every question. Dr. Smith said the questions are scored "with a yes or no," and she did not mention the do not know column. Question one asks whether there are previous conclusive reports on this reaction. Yes is plus one. She said this one is answered from the literature. Question two asks whether the adverse event appeared after the suspected drug was administered. Yes is plus two, and no is minus one. Question three asks whether the reaction improved when the drug was stopped or a specific antagonist was given. Yes is plus one. Question four asks whether the reaction reappeared when the drug was given again. Yes is plus two, and no is minus one. Question five asks whether other causes or drugs could on their own have caused the reaction. Yes is minus one, and no is plus two. Question six asks whether the reaction reappeared when a placebo was given. Yes is minus one, and no is plus one. Questions seven to ten each give plus one for yes. They ask about a toxic drug level in the blood or other fluids, a reaction that changed with the dose, a similar reaction on a previous exposure, and objective evidence. Dr. Smith pointed to questions two, three, and four as timing questions, and she counted question six as time related too. She said, "we have to think about the timing, the relationship of when they were put on this drug and when they started seeing the symptoms." She also said, "sometimes a yes is two points, sometimes it's one point, sometimes a no is negative." The points are added. The page prints four bands. A total of nine is definite, five to eight is probable, one to four is possible, and zero is doubtful. Dr. Smith said the rankings are "definite, probable, possible, or remote," so her word for the lowest band is remote. A total above nine or below zero is possible, and the page prints no band for it.
